title: My hut is roofed
hookLine: Subhuti: my hut is roofed and snug; rain, god, if you like (Theragatha 1.1)

lines: A ROOF, A MIND, A DARE.
A MONK IN A SMALL HUT.
HE TALKS BACK TO THE SKY.
cards: A roof, a mind, and a dare to the weather. A monk named Subhuti sits in a small hut, and what he says to the sky is the poem numbered first in the brothers' book.
It isn't a plea for the rain to stop, or a complaint about the leaks. It's closer to an invitation: freedom, talking back to the weather.

teach.h: A ROOF, SNUG AND OUT OF THE WIND.
teach.b: First, the hut. Subhuti says his hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind. A small thing, done well.
In the wet season, a good roof is the difference between sitting through the night and running for cover. Second, the mind.
In the same breath he says his mind is well settled, and freed. Two shelters side by side, both finished. One keeps the water out.
The other no longer lets the old storms in. Third, the dare.
So rain, god, if you like, he says. The poem speaks to the rain as a god, the one who sends it, and Subhuti isn't asking that god for anything. Rain, or don't.

teach.h: THE WHOLE BOOK IN A FEW LINES.
teach.b: Fourth, why it's a fitting door into the book. The poem is tiny, but it holds the whole Theragatha in small: the weather, a man alone, and the quiet news that the work is done. Some readers hear a little swagger in it.
Others hear relief, the voice of someone who used to dread the storm and doesn't anymore.
The poem doesn't say which, and it doesn't need to. A dry roof isn't nothing. Neither is a settled mind.
Put the two together and the sky can do what it likes.

how: Forest monks in the Theravada tradition still live in small huts called kutis, and teachers often read Subhuti's short poem as a picture of a mind at ease whatever the weather.

o: a begging bowl for collecting alms
a small hut where a forest monk lives
a rain cloak worn in the wet season

p: roofed, pleasant, out of the wind

s: Subhuti asks the rain to stop
he tells the rain-god to rain if he likes. his hut is roofed and his mind is settled.
the poem sets the hut and the mind side by side
two shelters, both finished: one keeps out the water, the other the old storms.
the opening poem of the brothers' book runs for pages

games.q: you're in a small forest hut and dark clouds are rolling in. what do you say to the sky?
o: rain, if you like. I'm covered.
I'd better find a stronger shelter.
games.why: Subhuti's hut is roofed and his mind is freed, so he dares the rain-god: rain, if you like.

practice: Sit snugly, as if it's raining, and if it is, listen to it; notice what's covering you right now, a chair at your back, a blanket on your knees, the walls around you.

Then turn to the mind and see what leaks in, a worry, a plan, a noise from the next room, and let it drip without fixing the roof. If you like, say Subhuti's words quietly to whatever's coming: rain, if you like.

wordCard.voice: Kuti. A hut, the forest monk's small dwelling: the shelter in Subhuti's opening words in the Theragatha, a settled mind inside, so let it rain. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: kuti, a hut, the small dwelling of a forest monk.

carryVoice: Your line: rain if you like. The brothers' book opens with only a few lines, and a mind at ease in the rain. See you tomorrow.
